name: E2B
oneLiner: Firecracker microVMs and templates for agent code, sold per running second.
whatItIs: E2B sells isolated sandboxes for agents: a Linux VM created on demand from a template, driven through Python and JavaScript SDKs. It is infrastructure for a product rather than a finished assistant.
Templates define what a sandbox starts with, including images built from Docker images, and the code-interpreter and desktop products run inside the sandbox.
whoFor: Developers integrating code execution, data analysis or computer use into an agent product.
isolation: Firecracker microVM with its own kernel, not a container. The default template user is `user`, not root; root can be set in a template. Docker is documented, but kernel features are not unlimited: the sandbox kernel does not ship `xt_owner`.
sizes: Sized by vCPU and RAM: up to 8 vCPU and 8 GiB self-serve (Pro is listed as 8+ by support request), and 10 or 20 GiB of included disk. No GPU on any plan. Regions: US (GCP), US West and US East (AWS), EU and APAC.

billing.model: Per-second usage against a credit balance; Pro adds a monthly plan fee.
billing.meter: $0.000014 per vCPU-second and $0.0000045 per GiB-second of allocated resources while running. Paused and killed sandboxes are not billed.
billing.stopped: Nothing for compute. Volumes and snapshots are separate objects with their own storage.
billing.planFee: Hobby has no fee; Pro is $150 a month plus usage; Enterprise starts at a $2,000 monthly commit including 500 concurrent sandboxes (the Markdown pricing page still says a $3,000 minimum).
billing.minimum: No published per-sandbox minimum. Hobby starts with a one-time $100 credit and no card.

well: A microVM with its own kernel, Docker, snapshots that keep memory, and up to 20 forks from a running sandbox.
An agent that needs a real API and SDKs, plus templates built from any Docker image.
A team that needs a SOC 2 report, with a HIPAA BAA on Enterprise plans.
badly: A long-running agent: the default timeout kills the sandbox after five minutes and commands do not reset it.
Memory above 8 GiB without asking support, or any GPU workload.
A client-facing link you can paste into a browser: private URLs need a header token, so sharing one still needs a proxy or a public sandbox.

usability.dashboard: A console exists for support and API keys, but the documented path is SDKs, a CLI and API keys.
usability.withoutCode: No documented no-code path. Examples are SDK calls, terminals and templates; the desktop SDK still needs code to drive it.
usability.signup: No credit card to start, and a one-time $100 credit. When a workspace without a payment method runs out, every project in it is blocked shortly afterwards.
usability.docs: Extensive docs with per-page Markdown. Support is through the console. SOC 2 Type II is reported, and a HIPAA BAA is available on Enterprise plans.
tripsUp: The default timeout is 5 minutes and the default action is to kill the sandbox.
New projects are private by URL, but older projects stay public until an owner changes the setting, and the token is a header rather than part of the link.
Three pages give three different default sandbox sizes.
Volumes are in private beta and cannot be snapshotted.

caveats.issue: The default timeout destroys the sandbox
caveats.detail: Every sandbox has a timeout defaulting to five minutes, and `onTimeout: 'kill'` is the default. Pausing instead is opt-in.

caveats.issue: The default sandbox size is stated three ways
caveats.detail: The pricing page says the default is 2 vCPU / 4 GiB; the billing docs say 2 vCPU / 512 MiB; the template build limits say a rebuilt template gets 2 vCPU / 1024 MiB. All three are current provider statements; this guide prices explicit shapes, so only the default prose is affected.

evidence.quote: The default sandbox has 2 vCPUs and 4 GiB of RAM.
Start with default resources (2 vCPU, 512 MiB RAM)
Rebuilding without them writes the defaults of 2 vCPU and 1024 MiB

caveats.detail: Volumes persist across sandboxes but file locking can hang, handles can go stale, mounts are fixed at creation, and snapshots and read-only mounts are not supported.

caveats.issue: No static egress IP on any plan
caveats.detail: There are no dedicated or static egress addresses, including Enterprise. BYOP, which routes egress through a SOCKS5 proxy you run, is the documented way to get a stable address.

caveats.issue: Older projects keep public URLs by default
caveats.detail: Since 30 October 2026 new projects default to private sandbox traffic behind a per-sandbox e2b-traffic-access-token header. Existing projects stay public until an owner changes the setting, and the token is a header, so a plain browser link still needs a proxy.

The rendered pricing page says Enterprise starts at a $2,000 monthly commit with 500 concurrent sandboxes; the Markdown twin of the same page still says a $3,000 monthly minimum. This guide uses the rendered page, which changed most recently.

evidence.quote: Enterprise starts at a $2,000/mo commit, 500 concurrent included.
A $3,000 monthly minimum applies to Enterprise usage.

caveats.issue: SSO and SCIM: described, and also called planned
caveats.detail: The workspace docs describe how workspaces with SSO or SCIM behave, while the enterprise page says SSO, SCIM and RBAC are planned. This guide treats SSO and SCIM as existing but undocumented.

evidence.quote: **Workspaces with SSO or SCIM** have invites disabled.
SSO, SCIM, and RBAC are planned; ask E2B about timelines.

strengths: Snapshots capture memory and filesystem, and the source keeps running.
Fork up to 20 sandboxes from a running VM, with a documented pause.
Templates can start from any Docker image.
Secrets can be injected outside the VM by an egress proxy.
SOC 2 Type II, with a HIPAA BAA on Enterprise plans.
Private-by-default sandbox URLs with a per-sandbox traffic token for new projects.
Ready-made templates for Claude Code, Codex, Amp, OpenCode, Hermes, OpenClaw and four more agents.
